newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania flashy "Gypsy King" dies of heart attack.
newsitem.headline: Romania flashy "Gypsy King" dies of heart attack.

text.p: Romania's self-styled "Gypsy King" Ion Cioaba, who claimed to rule over the Balkan country's last nomads, died late on Sunday of a heart attack in a Bucharest hospital, aged 62.
"Cioaba's death is a big loss to us. He was a wise man and highly active in politics," said his rival Iulian Radulescu, self-proclaimed "Emperor of Gypsies Everywhere".

Romania has 410,000 Gypsies according to census data, but leaders say the community is much bigger. Gypsies were repressed under the ousted Communists, who treated them as second-class citizens and parasites.
Cioaba and Radulescu shared flashy lifestyles in their Transylvanian fiefdom of Sibiu.
Mercedes and Cadillac motorcades, a two-floor villa with marble stairs and modern furniture were Cioaba's style.
Cioaba proclaimed himself "King" of Romanian Gypsies in a church ceremony in 1992, taking advantage of new freedom of expression following the fall of communism in 1989.
Subsequently, he added to his bejewelled solid-gold crown the white cloak and insignia of a member of the order of "Knights Templar", abolished hundreds of years ago.
Cioaba ran for his Party of Nomadic Roma (Gypsies) and Tinkers in last November's elections, but failed to get a seat on parliament's upper Senate.
"Cioaba's death ends a chapter in our community's history," said Madalin Voicu, who represents one of Romania's several Gypsy parties in the lower Chamber of Deputies.
"He loved justice and truth, as he loved his country and its people, be they Romanians or Gyspies," said his daughter Luminita, the author of volumes of poetry on Gypsies' life.

Historic tradition has it that Mongols and Tartars brought the first Gypsies to Romania in 1242 as slaves, and sold them to Romanians. Nomadic gypsies wandered here from India in the 15th century, bringing their skills as copper- and goldsmiths.

"I don't know whether there will be a successor to the throne. What the community needs is a person to continue his (Cioaba's) struggle for our rights and statute," Voicu said. Cioaba is outlived by his wife, one son and five daughters. His son Florin will succeed him, according to Gypsy tradition.
